title: Moog Taurus I Foot-Operated Bass Synthesizer
subtitle: An analog synthesizer with no keyboard at all — pitch is chosen with the feet on a spinet-organ-style pedal board while the hands play other instruments
why_scout_cares: The Moog Taurus is the museum's cleanest keyboard-less synthesizer and its clearest 'lower body as an input channel' instrument: instead of pressing keys with the hands, the player chooses pitches with 13 foot pedals on an organ-style pedal board, freeing both hands to play other keyboards. Designed by Moog's Director of Engineering David Luce for the never-released Constellation ensemble, the Taurus I (1975-1981) is an embodied split of labor across the body — feet own the bass line, hands own everything else — that inverted the conventional position of a keyboard instrument. Its pure-controller descendant (the 343C Taurus II Controller) even shipped with no synth module at all, just CV/gate foot outputs. The interaction model (foot-as-pitch-selection) has no near neighbor in the museum and the instrument is image-rich on Commons at high resolution.

research.title: Moog Taurus I Foot-Operated Bass Synthesizer
research.overview:
The Moog Taurus is a foot-operated analog synthesizer designed and manufactured by Moog Music. The original Taurus I was produced from 1975 to 1981. It was conceived as part of Moog's Constellation series of synthesizers — a bass instrument meant to be played by foot while the player's hands handled one or more keyboards. Instead of a conventional keyboard, the Taurus uses a 13-pedal organ-style pedal board similar to the pedal keyboard of a spinet organ. The sound-shaping controls are protected by a removable plastic window so they cannot be accidentally adjusted mid-performance.

The Taurus I is monophonic and monotimbral, with two oscillators driving a 24 dB/octave resonant low-pass filter through a three-stage VCA; the usable waveform is a distorted sawtooth. It stored three presets plus one user setting. Because the Taurus was designed to sit at the player's feet, the interaction is fundamentally embodied: the bass line is performed with the lower body while the hands are elsewhere. The Constellation configuration was famously used on the 1973 Emerson, Lake & Palmer album Brain Salad Surgery, though the full set was never released commercially.

The Taurus I became a staple of 1970s-80s progressive rock (Genesis, Rush, Yes, Pink Floyd, U2, The Police) and reached top-40 radio via Phil Collins's 'I Don't Care Anymore'. A control-only variant, the model 343C Taurus II Controller, shipped CV & gate outputs with no synth module at all — a pure foot-driven pitch/gate input device. The Taurus II (1981-1983) raised the control panel for manual access during performance and offered 18 pedals.

deepDive.heading: Feet as the pitch-selection interface
deepDive.text: Where keyboards put pitch under the fingers, the Taurus puts it under the feet. The player chooses notes with a 13-pedal spinet-organ pedal board (the I and III) or 18 pedals (the II), leaving both hands free for other instruments. This is a radical reallocation of a musical control channel across the body — the bass line becomes a lower-limb gesture. The removable plastic window over the sound-shaping controls reinforced the design intent: the machine is set up, then played feet-first without reaching down for tweaks mid-song.

deepDive.heading: The controller without a brain
deepDive.text: The Taurus II era produced a telling variant: the 343C Taurus II Controller shipped with CV & gate outputs and no synthesizer module at all. It is purely a foot-input device — a standalone pitch/gate controller reading muscle movement of the feet and sending control voltages to other gear. This makes the foot-pedal interface the abstract and reusable part of the design, an early example of splitting the input surface from the sound source.

deepDive.heading: An intended quartet never released
deepDive.text: The Taurus was designed for the Constellation: a monophonic bass (Taurus), a monophonic lead (Lyra), and a polyphonic keyboard (Apollo), all played simultaneously by one person. The Apollo was redesigned into the Moog Polymoog (1975-1980) and the Taurus I released standalone, but the Lyra (designed by Robert Moog himself) was never commercially released. The museum's Collection entry captures the piece as a standalone realization of that multi-body, one-performer ensemble idea.
